claim: European colonization of the Americas resulted in a dramatic population collapse of the Indigenous inhabitants caused in part by the introduction of new pathogens.
source: After the European colonization of the Americas, there was a dramatic population collapse of the Indigenous inhabitants caused in part by the introduction of new pathogens.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Acuña-Soto et al., 2004; Lindo et al., 2016).

claim: Three ancient human parvovirus B19 genomes were reconstructed from distinct individuals from Colonial Mexico.
source: This allowed us to reconstruct three ancient human parvovirus B19 genomes and one ancient human hepatitis B virus genome from distinct individuals.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figure 2b shows the reconstructed B19V genomes with coverage and depth data.

claim: One ancient human hepatitis B virus genome was reconstructed from a Colonial Mexico individual.
source: This allowed us to reconstruct three ancient human parvovirus B19 genomes and one ancient human hepatitis B virus genome from distinct individuals.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figure 2c shows the reconstructed HBV genome with coverage and depth data.

claim: The reconstructed viral genomes are similar to African strains.
source: The viral genomes are similar to African strains, consistent with the inferred morphological and genetic African ancestry of the hosts as well as with the isotopic analysis of the human remains, suggesting an origin on the African continent.
evidence: The abstract states this, and phylogenetic analyses in Figure 3 show clustering with African viral strains.

claim: The hosts of the reconstructed viruses had African ancestry based on morphological and genetic analysis.
source: The viral genomes are similar to African strains, consistent with the inferred morphological and genetic African ancestry of the hosts as well as with the isotopic analysis of the human remains, suggesting an origin on the African continent.
evidence: Figure 4a shows PCA analysis placing individuals within African genetic variation, and morphological features were used for sample selection.

claim: Isotopic analysis of human remains suggests an African origin for the hosts.
source: The viral genomes are similar to African strains, consistent with the inferred morphological and genetic African ancestry of the hosts as well as with the isotopic analysis of the human remains, suggesting an origin on the African continent.
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows 87Sr/86Sr ratios from tooth enamel consistent with West African values.

claim: Ancient viruses were transported to the Americas during the transatlantic slave trade.
source: This study provides direct molecular evidence of ancient viruses being transported to the Americas during the transatlantic slave trade and their subsequent introduction to New Spain.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion based on the combination of viral phylogenetic data, host ancestry analysis, and isotopic evidence.

claim: Viral diseases such as smallpox, measles, and mumps have been proposed to be responsible for many devastating epidemics during the Colonial period.
source: Among these pathogens, viral diseases, such as smallpox, measles, and mumps, have been proposed to be responsible for many of the devastating epidemics during the Colonial period (Acuña-Soto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Acuña-Soto et al., 2004.

claim: The pathogen(s) responsible for the deadliest epidemics in New Spain remains unknown and is thought to have caused millions of deaths during the 16th century.
source: Remarkably, the pathogen(s) responsible for the deadliest epidemics reported in New Spain (the Spanish viceroyalty that corresponds to Mexico, Central America, and the current US southwest states) remains unknown and is thought to have caused millions of deaths during the 16th century (Acuña-Soto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Acuña-Soto et al., 2004.

claim: Indigenous populations were drastically affected by Cocoliztli epidemics, followed by Africans and to a lesser extent European people.
source: Indigenous populations were drastically affected by these mysterious epidemics, generically referred to as Cocoliztli ('pest' in Nahuatl), followed by Africans and to a lesser extent European people (Acuña-Soto et al., 2004; Malvido and Viesca, 1982; Somolinos d'Árdois, 1982).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to historical sources.

claim: The Hospital Real de San José de los Naturales was the first hospital in Mexico dedicated specifically to treat the Indigenous population.
source: Accounts of the 1576 Cocoliztli epidemic were described in autopsy reports of victims treated at the 'Hospital Real de San José de los Naturales' (HSJN) (Malvido and Viesca, 1982; Wesp, 2017), the first hospital in Mexico dedicated specifically to treat the Indigenous population (Malvido and Viesca, 1982; Wesp, 2017; Figure 1a and b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Malvido and Viesca, 1982; Wesp, 2017.

claim: A recent paleogenomics study reported a sub-Saharan African origin of three individuals from the HSJN collection.
source: Indeed, a recent paleogenomics study reported a sub-Saharan African origin of three individuals from this collection (Barquera et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Barquera et al., 2020.

claim: Twenty-one dental samples from HSJN were selected based on morphometric analyses and dental modifications that suggested African ancestry.
source: For the HSJN, 21 dental samples (premolar and molar teeth) were selected based on previous morphometric analyses and dental modifications that suggested an African ancestry (Hernández-Lopez and Negrete, 2012; Karam-Tapia, 2012; Meza, 2013; Ruíz-Albarrán, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to morphometric studies.

claim: Metagenomic analyses revealed 17 samples containing at least one normalized hit to viral DNA.
source: Metagenomic analyses with MALT (Herbig et al., 2018) (Materials and methods) on the NGS data using the Viral NCBI RefSeq database as a reference (Pruitt et al., 2007) revealed 17 samples containing at least one normalized hit to viral DNA (abundances were normalized to the smallest library since each sample had different number of reads) (Materials and methods), particularly similar to Hepadnaviridae, Herpesviridae, Parvoviridae, and Poxviridae viral families (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A customized enrichment assay targeting ancient DNA from viruses of clinical importance was designed and applied.
source: To uncover the diversity of viral pathogens during this period, we designed an enrichment assay targeting ancient DNA (aDNA) from viruses of clinical importance and applied it to DNA extracts from individuals found in a Colonial hospital and a Colonial chapel (16th–18th century) where records suggest that victims of epidemics were buried during important outbreaks in Mexico City.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and detailed in the Materials and methods section with Supplementary file 1A showing the probe design.

claim: One post-capture library had an ~100-fold increase of Hepadnaviridae-like hits (HBV).
source: Only one post-capture library had an ~100-fold increase of Hepadnaviridae-like hits (HBV), while three more libraries had an ~50–200-fold increase of Parvoviridae-like hits (B19V) (Figure 1c, Supplementary file 1B), compared to their corresponding pre-capture libraries (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1c and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: Three libraries had an ~50–200-fold increase of Parvoviridae-like hits (B19V).
source: Only one post-capture library had an ~100-fold increase of Hepadnaviridae-like hits (HBV), while three more libraries had an ~50–200-fold increase of Parvoviridae-like hits (B19V) (Figure 1c, Supplementary file 1B), compared to their corresponding pre-capture libraries (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1c and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: The captured negative control (HSJN177) presented negligible enrichment of viral hits.
source: In contrast, the captured negative control (HSJN177) presented a negligible enrichment of these viral hits (Figure 1c, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The reconstructed viral reads showed an accumulation of C to T mutations towards their 5′ terminal site with an almost symmetrical G to A pattern on the 3′ end, as expected for ancient DNA.
source: To confirm the ancient origin of these viral reads, we evaluated the misincorporation damage patterns using the program mapDamage 2.0 (Jónsson et al., 2013), which revealed an accumulation of C to T mutations towards their 5′ terminal site with an almost symmetrical G to A pattern on the 3′ end (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as expected for aDNA (Briggs et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and cited to Briggs et al., 2007.

claim: Three ancient B19V genomes were reconstructed with sequence coverages between 92.37% and 99.1%, and average depths of 2.98–15.36× along their single-stranded DNA coding region.
source: Three ancient B19V genomes were reconstructed (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 1C) with sequence coverages between 92.37% and 99.1%, and average depths of 2.98–15.36× along their single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) coding region, which excludes the double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) hairpin regions at each end of the genome (Luo and Qiu, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2b and Supplementary file 1C.

claim: The dsDNA inverse terminal repeats (ITRs) of B19V displayed considerably higher depth values (<218×) compared to the coding region.
source: These dsDNA inverse terminal repeats (ITRs) displayed considerably higher depth values (<218×) compared to the coding region consistent with the better postmortem preservation of dsDNA compared to ssDNA (Lindahl, 1993; Figure 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2b and cited to Lindahl, 1993.

claim: One ancient HBV genome was reconstructed at 30.8× average depth and with a sequence coverage of 89.9%.
source: In addition, we reconstructed one ancient HBV genome (Figure 2c, Supplementary file 1C) at 30.8× average depth and with a sequence coverage of 89.9%, including its ssDNA region at a reduced depth (<10×).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2c and Supplementary file 1C.

claim: The reconstructed ancient HBV genome shows a 6 nucleotide insertion in the core gene, which is characteristic of genotype A.
source: The reconstructed ancient HBV genome shows a 6 nucleotide (nt) insertion in the core gene, which is characteristic of the genotype A (Kramvis, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Kramvis, 2014.

claim: The Colonial HBV genome clustered with modern sequences corresponding to sub-genotype A4.
source: Further phylogenetic analyses (Materials and methods) revealed that the Colonial HBV genome clustered with modern sequences corresponding to sub-genotype A4 (previously named A6) (Pourkarim et al., 2014; Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and cited to Pourkarim et al., 2014.

claim: HBV genotype A has a broad diversity in Africa reflecting its long history in this continent.
source: The genotype A (HBV/GtA) has a broad diversity in Africa reflecting its long history in this continent (Kostaki et al., 2018; Kramvis, 2014), while the sub-genotype A4 has been recovered uniquely from African individuals in Belgium (Pourkarim et al., 2010) and has never been found in the Americas.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Kostaki et al., 2018; Kramvis, 2014.

claim: HBV sub-genotype A4 has been recovered uniquely from African individuals in Belgium and has never been found in the Americas.
source: The genotype A (HBV/GtA) has a broad diversity in Africa reflecting its long history in this continent (Kostaki et al., 2018; Kramvis, 2014), while the sub-genotype A4 has been recovered uniquely from African individuals in Belgium (Pourkarim et al., 2010) and has never been found in the Americas.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Pourkarim et al., 2010.

claim: The three Colonial B19V genomes were phylogenetically closer to modern B19V sequences belonging to genotype 3.
source: Regarding the three Colonial B19V genomes from individuals HSJN240, COYC4, and HSJNC81 (C81A), these were phylogenetically closer to modern B19V sequences belonging to genotype 3 (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3.

claim: B19V genotype 3 is divided into two sub-genotypes: 3a, which is mostly found in Africa, and 3b, which is proposed to have spread outside Africa recently.
source: This B19V genotype is divided into two sub-genotypes: 3a, which is mostly found in Africa, and 3b, which is proposed to have spread outside Africa recently (Hübschen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Hübschen et al., 2009.

claim: The viral sequences from individuals HSJN240 and COYC4 are similar to sub-genotype 3b genomes sampled from immigrants in Germany.
source: The viral sequences from the individuals HSJN240 and COYC4 are similar to sub-genotype 3b genomes sampled from immigrants (Morocco, Egypt, and Turkey) in Germany (Schneider et al., 2008; Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3) while the sequence of the individual HSJNC81 is more similar to a divergent sub-genotype 3a strain (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3) retrieved from a child with severe anemia born in France (Nguyen et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Schneider et al., 2008 and reference to Figure 3b.

claim: The sequence of individual HSJNC81 is more similar to a divergent sub-genotype 3a strain retrieved from a child with severe anemia born in France.
source: The viral sequences from the individuals HSJN240 and COYC4 are similar to sub-genotype 3b genomes sampled from immigrants (Morocco, Egypt, and Turkey) in Germany (Schneider et al., 2008; Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3) while the sequence of the individual HSJNC81 is more similar to a divergent sub-genotype 3a strain (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3) retrieved from a child with severe anemia born in France (Nguyen et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Nguyen et al., 1999 and reference to Figure 3b.

claim: A temporal structure was identified for B19V when including all three genotypes (R2 = 0.3837; correlation coefficient = 0.6194).
source: In the case of B19V, we identified a temporal structure when including all three genotypes (R2 = 0.3837; correlation coefficient = 0.6194) (Figure 3—figure supplement 6a-c), in agreement with previous studies (Mühlemann et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 6a-c and citation to Mühlemann et al., 2018b.

claim: A median substitution rate for B19V of 1.03 × 10–5 (95% HPD: 8.66 × 10–6–1.21 × 10–5) s/s/y was inferred under a strict clock and a constant population prior.
source: We inferred a median substitution rate for B19V of 1.03 × 10–5 (95% HPD: 8.66 × 10–6–1.21 × 10–5) s/s/y under a strict clock and a constant population prior, and a substitution rate of 2.62 × 10–5 (95% HPD: 1.50 × 10–5–3.98 × 10–5) s/s/y under a relaxed log normal clock and a constant population prior.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on dated coalescent phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The divergence times from the most recent common ancestor of B19V genotypes 1, 2, and 3 under a strict clock were 7.19 (95% HPD: 6.98–7.46), 2.11 (95% HPD: 1.83–2.51), and 3.64 (95% HPD: 3.04–4.33) ka, respectively.
source: The divergence times from the most recent common ancestor of genotypes 1, 2, and 3 under a strict clock were 7.19 (95% HPD: 6.98–7.46), 2.11 (95% HPD: 1.83–2.51), and 3.64 (95% HPD: 3.04–4.33) ka, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on dated coalescent phylogenetic analysis.

claim: All three HSJN individuals from which the reconstructed viral genomes were isolated fall within African genetic variation in a principal component analysis plot.
source: The nuclear genetic ancestry analysis showed that all three HSJN individuals, from which the reconstructed viral genomes were isolated, fall within African genetic variation in a principal component analysis (PCA) plot (Figure 4a), while their mitochondrial aDNA belong to the L haplogroup, which has high frequency in African populations (Supplementary file 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4a.

claim: The mitochondrial aDNA of the three HSJN individuals belong to the L haplogroup, which has high frequency in African populations.
source: The nuclear genetic ancestry analysis showed that all three HSJN individuals, from which the reconstructed viral genomes were isolated, fall within African genetic variation in a principal component analysis (PCA) plot (Figure 4a), while their mitochondrial aDNA belong to the L haplogroup, which has high frequency in African populations (Supplementary file 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Supplementary file 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The 87Sr/86Sr ratios measured on the enamel of individual HSJNC81 (0.71098) and HSJN240 (0.71109) are similar to average 87Sr/86Sr ratios found in soils and rocks from West Africa.
source: The 87Sr/86Sr ratios measured on the enamel of the individual HSJNC81 (0.71098) and HSJN240 (0.71109) are similar to average 87Sr/86Sr ratios found in soils and rocks from West Africa (average of 0.71044, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2), as well as to 87Sr/86Sr ratios described in first-generation Africans in the Americas (Barquera et al., 2020; Bastos et al., 2016; Fricke et al., 2020; Price et al., 2012; Schroeder et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2, and citations to multiple studies.

claim: The 87Sr/86Sr ratios on the parietal and phalange bones from HSJNC81 (0.70672) and HSJN240 (0.70755) show lower values similar to those observed in the Trans Mexican Volcanic Belt where the Mexico City Valley is located.
source: In contrast, the 87Sr/86Sr ratios on the parietal and phalange bones from the HSJNC81 (0.70672) and HSJN240 (0.70755) show lower values similar to those observed in the Trans Mexican Volcanic Belt where the Mexico City Valley is located (0.70420–0.70550, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Radiocarbon dating of HSJN240 (1442–1608 CE, years calibrated for 1σ) and HSJN194 (1472–1625 CE, years calibrated for 1σ) indicates that these individuals arrived during the first decades of the Colonial period.
source: Moreover, radiocarbon dating of HSJN240 (1442–1608 CE, years calibrated for 1σ) and HSJN194 (1472–1625 CE, years calibrated for 1σ) (Supplementary file 2A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) indicates that these individuals arrived during the first decades of the Colonial period, when the number of enslaved individuals arriving from Africa was particularly high (Aguirre-Beltrán, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Supplementary file 2A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and citation to Aguirre-Beltrán, 2005.

claim: Colonial individual COYC4 clusters with present-day Mexicans and Peruvians from the 1000 Genomes Project.
source: Strikingly, Colonial individual COYC4, who was also infected with an African B19V strain, clusters with present-day Mexicans and Peruvians from the 1000 Genomes Project (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4a.

claim: An ADMIXTURE analysis confirmed a Native American genetic component in individual COYC4.
source: An ADMIXTURE (Alexander and Lange, 2011) analysis with these data confirmed a Native American genetic component (Figure 4b), as expected for an indigenous individual.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4b and citation to Alexander and Lange, 2011.

claim: The B19V ancient genome from individual COYC4 is the first genotype 3 genome obtained from a non-African individual.
source: The B19V ancient genome from the individual COYC4 is the first genotype 3 genome obtained from a non-African individual and suggests that following the introduction from Africa, the virus (B19V) spread and infected people of different ancestries during the Colonial period.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Following the introduction from Africa, B19V spread and infected people of different ancestries during the Colonial period.
source: The B19V ancient genome from the individual COYC4 is the first genotype 3 genome obtained from a non-African individual and suggests that following the introduction from Africa, the virus (B19V) spread and infected people of different ancestries during the Colonial period.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the finding of B19V genotype 3 in an individual with Native American ancestry.

claim: B19V and HBV are blood-borne human pathogens that are not present in soil or the environment.
source: Moreover, it is important to notice that B19V and HBV are blood-borne human pathogens that are not present in soil or the environment, and that DNA from these viruses had never been extracted before in the aDNA facilities used for this study.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: DNA from B19V and HBV had never been extracted before in the aDNA facilities used for this study.
source: Moreover, it is important to notice that B19V and HBV are blood-borne human pathogens that are not present in soil or the environment, and that DNA from these viruses had never been extracted before in the aDNA facilities used for this study.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: dsDNA intermediates form during the B19V replication cycle.
source: However, it is known that dsDNA intermediates form during the B19V replication cycle (Ganaie and Qiu, 2018), and that throughout the viral infection the replicating genomes are present in both the ssDNA and dsDNA forms.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Ganaie and Qiu, 2018.

claim: Throughout the B19V viral infection, the replicating genomes are present in both the ssDNA and dsDNA forms.
source: However, it is known that dsDNA intermediates form during the B19V replication cycle (Ganaie and Qiu, 2018), and that throughout the viral infection the replicating genomes are present in both the ssDNA and dsDNA forms.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Ganaie and Qiu, 2018.

claim: The sequences retrieved from B19V must correspond to the cell-free dsDNA replication intermediates.
source: The sequences we retrieved must therefore correspond to the cell-free dsDNA replication intermediates.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the library construction method and knowledge of B19V replication.

claim: HBV and B19V are capable of integrating into the human host genome.
source: Although HBV and B19V are also capable of integrating into the human host genome (Yuen et al., 2018; Janovitz et al., 2017), the uneven read coverage observed for all reconstructed viruses (higher coverage in dsDNA regions) suggests that these sequences do not correspond to integration events.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Yuen et al., 2018; Janovitz et al., 2017.

claim: The uneven read coverage observed for all reconstructed viruses suggests that these sequences do not correspond to integration events.
source: Although HBV and B19V are also capable of integrating into the human host genome (Yuen et al., 2018; Janovitz et al., 2017), the uneven read coverage observed for all reconstructed viruses (higher coverage in dsDNA regions) suggests that these sequences do not correspond to integration events.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the coverage patterns shown in Figure 2.

claim: B19V genotype 3 is most prevalent in West Africa (Ghana: 100%, n = 11; Burkina Faso: 100%, n = 5).
source: This genotype is most prevalent in West Africa (Ghana: 100%, n = 11; Burkina Faso: 100%, n = 5) (Candotti et al., 2004; Hübschen et al., 2009; Rinckel et al., 2009) and a potential African origin has been suggested (Candotti et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Candotti et al., 2004; Hübschen et al., 2009; Rinckel et al., 2009.

claim: A potential African origin has been suggested for B19V genotype 3.
source: This genotype is most prevalent in West Africa (Ghana: 100%, n = 11; Burkina Faso: 100%, n = 5) (Candotti et al., 2004; Hübschen et al., 2009; Rinckel et al., 2009) and a potential African origin has been suggested (Candotti et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Candotti et al., 2004.

claim: B19V genotype 3 has been sporadically found outside of Africa in Brazil (50%, n = 12), India (15.4%, n = 13), France (11.4%, n = 79), and the USA (0.85%, n = 117).
source: It has also been sporadically found outside of Africa (Jain et al., 2015),(Candotti et al., 2004; Rinckel et al., 2009) in Brazil (50%, n = 12) (Freitas et al., 2008; Sanabani et al., 2006), India (15.4%, n = 13) (Jain et al., 2015), France (11.4%, n = 79) (Nguyen et al., 1999; Servant et al., 2002), and the USA (0.85%, n = 117) (Rinckel et al., 2009) as well as in immigrants from Morocco, Egypt, and Turkey in Germany (6.7%, n = 59) (Schneider et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with multiple citations.

claim: B19V genotype 1 is the most common and is found worldwide.
source: Two other genotypes, 1 and 2, exist for this virus. Genotype 1 is the most common and is found worldwide, while the almost extinct genotype 2 is mainly found in elderly people from Northern Europe (Pyöriä et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Pyöriä et al., 2017.

claim: B19V genotype 2 is almost extinct and is mainly found in elderly people from Northern Europe.
source: Two other genotypes, 1 and 2, exist for this virus. Genotype 1 is the most common and is found worldwide, while the almost extinct genotype 2 is mainly found in elderly people from Northern Europe (Pyöriä et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Pyöriä et al., 2017.

claim: Ancient genomes from B19V genotypes 1 and 2 have been recovered from Eurasian samples, including a genotype 2 B19V genome from a 10th-century Viking burial in Greenland.
source: Ancient genomes from genotypes 1 and 2 have been recovered from Eurasian samples, including a genotype 2 B19V genome from a 10th-century Viking burial in Greenland (Mühlemann et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Mühlemann et al., 2018b.

claim: 87Sr/86Sr isotopes on individuals from a Viking burial in Greenland revealed that they were immigrants from Iceland.
source: 87Sr/86Sr isotopes on individuals from this burial revealed that they were immigrants from Iceland (Mühlemann et al., 2018b), suggesting an introduction of the genotype 2 to North America during Viking explorations of Greenland.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Mühlemann et al., 2018b.

claim: Serological evidence indicates that B19V currently circulates in Mexico.
source: While serological evidence indicates that B19V currently circulates in Mexico, only the presence of genotype 1 has been formally described using molecular analyses (Valencia Pacheco et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Valencia Pacheco et al., 2017.

claim: Only the presence of B19V genotype 1 has been formally described in Mexico using molecular analyses.
source: While serological evidence indicates that B19V currently circulates in Mexico, only the presence of genotype 1 has been formally described using molecular analyses (Valencia Pacheco et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Valencia Pacheco et al., 2017.

claim: The introduction of HBV genotype A from Africa to the Americas has been proposed based on phylogenetic analysis of modern strains from Brazil and Mexico.
source: The introduction of the genotype A from Africa to the Americas has been proposed based on phylogenetic analysis of modern strains from Brazil (Freitas et al., 2008; Kostaki et al., 2018) and Mexico (Roman et al., 2010), and more precisely of the sub-genotype A1 using sequences from Martinique (Brichler et al., 2013), Venezuela (Quintero et al., 2002), Haiti (Andernach et al., 2009), and Colombia (Alvarado-Mora et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with multiple citations.

claim: A similar introduction pattern was proposed for the quasi genotype A3 based on an ancient HBV genome recovered from an ancient African individual sampled in Mexico.
source: Recently, a similar introduction pattern was proposed for the quasi genotype A3 based on an ancient HBV genome recovered from an ancient African individual sampled in Mexico (Barquera et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Barquera et al., 2020.

claim: The Colonial ancient HBV genome reconstructed represents the first ancient A4 linked to the transatlantic slave trade.
source: The Colonial ancient HBV genome reconstructed in our work represents the first ancient A4 linked to the transatlantic slave trade (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and the only report of this sub-genotype in the Americas, further supporting its African origin.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Colonial ancient HBV genome is the only report of sub-genotype A4 in the Americas.
source: The Colonial ancient HBV genome reconstructed in our work represents the first ancient A4 linked to the transatlantic slave trade (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and the only report of this sub-genotype in the Americas, further supporting its African origin.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The introduction of pathogens from Africa to the Americas has been proposed for smallpox based on historical records.
source: The introduction of pathogens from Africa to the Americas has been proposed for other human-infecting viruses such as smallpox (Mandujano-Sánchez et al., 1982; Somolinos d'Árdois, 1982), based on historical records; or yellow fever virus (Bryant et al., 2007), HTLMV-1 (Gadelha et al., 2014), hepatitis C virus (genotype 2) (Markov et al., 2009), and human herpes simplex virus (Forni et al., 2020) based on phylogenetic analysis of modern strains from Afro-descendant or admixed human populations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Mandujano-Sánchez et al., 1982; Somolinos d'Árdois, 1982.

claim: The introduction of yellow fever virus, HTLMV-1, hepatitis C virus (genotype 2), and human herpes simplex virus from Africa to the Americas has been proposed based on phylogenetic analysis of modern strains from Afro-descendant or admixed human populations.
source: The introduction of pathogens from Africa to the Americas has been proposed for other human-infecting viruses such as smallpox (Mandujano-Sánchez et al., 1982; Somolinos d'Árdois, 1982), based on historical records; or yellow fever virus (Bryant et al., 2007), HTLMV-1 (Gadelha et al., 2014), hepatitis C virus (genotype 2) (Markov et al., 2009), and human herpes simplex virus (Forni et al., 2020) based on phylogenetic analysis of modern strains from Afro-descendant or admixed human populations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Bryant et al., 2007; Gadelha et al., 2014; Markov et al., 2009; Forni et al., 2020.

claim: Individual HSJNC81 displayed cribra orbitalia in the eye sockets and porotic hyperostosis on the cranial vault.
source: Notably, individual HSJNC81 displayed cribra orbitalia in the eye sockets and porotic hyperostosis on the cranial vault (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The reconstructed ancient B19V genome from HSJNC81 is closest to the V9 strain, which was isolated from an infant with severe anemia and G6PD deficiency.
source: The reconstructed ancient B19V genome from this individual is closest to the V9 strain, which was isolated from an infant with severe anemia and G6PD deficiency (Nguyen et al., 1999; GenBank: AJ249437; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Nguyen et al., 1999 and reference to Figure 3b.

claim: The HSJN skeletal collection has a notably higher rate of cribra orbitalia and porotic hyperostosis compared to other Colonial archeological sites.
source: The HSJN skeletal collection has a notably higher rate of cribra orbitalia and porotic hyperostosis compared to other Colonial archeological sites, marks that were proposed to be caused by an unknown infectious disease (Castillo-Chavez, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Castillo-Chavez, 2000.

claim: Cribra orbitalia and porotic hyperostosis are caused by irregular hematopoiesis in the bone marrow and are typically associated with genetic anemias such as thalassemia and sickle cell anemia, as well as to nutritional stress or parasitic infections.
source: These skeletal indicators are caused by irregular hematopoiesis in the bone marrow and are typically associated with genetic anemias such as thalassemia and sickle cell anemia (Angel, 1966), as well as to nutritional stress or parasitic infections (Walker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Angel, 1966; Walker et al., 2009.

claim: B19V infection can cause severe or even fatal anemia due to the low level of hemoglobin in individuals with other blood disorders, such as thalassemia, sickle cell anemia, malaria, or iron deficiency.
source: It is acknowledged that B19V infection can cause severe or even fatal anemia due to the low level of hemoglobin in individuals with other blood disorders, such as thalassemia, sickle cell anemia, malaria, or iron deficiency (Broliden et al., 2006; Heegaard and Brown, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Broliden et al., 2006; Heegaard and Brown, 2002.

claim: B19V infects precursors of the erythroid lineage.
source: Therefore, since B19V infects precursors of the erythroid lineage (Broliden et al., 2006), it is possible that the morphological changes found in HSJNC81 might be the result of a severe anemia caused or enhanced by a B19V infection.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Broliden et al., 2006.

claim: It is possible that the morphological changes found in HSJNC81 might be the result of a severe anemia caused or enhanced by a B19V infection.
source: Therefore, since B19V infects precursors of the erythroid lineage (Broliden et al., 2006), it is possible that the morphological changes found in HSJNC81 might be the result of a severe anemia caused or enhanced by a B19V infection.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation based on the skeletal pathology and B19V infection.

claim: Several recent reports reveal that measles-like cases were actually attributable to B19V or rubella.
source: Nevertheless, the identification of ancient B19V in a Colonial context is noteworthy considering several recent reports reveal that measles-like cases were actually attributable to B19V (De Los Ángeles Ribas et al., 2019; Rezaei et al., 2016) or rubella (Anderson et al., 1985; Davidkin et al., 1998; De Los Ángeles Ribas et al., 2019; Rezaei et al., 2016), which produce a similar kind of rash and fever.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to De Los Ángeles Ribas et al., 2019; Rezaei et al., 2016; Anderson et al., 1985; Davidkin et al., 1998.

claim: B19V and rubella produce a similar kind of rash and fever to measles.
source: Nevertheless, the identification of ancient B19V in a Colonial context is noteworthy considering several recent reports reveal that measles-like cases were actually attributable to B19V (De Los Ángeles Ribas et al., 2019; Rezaei et al., 2016) or rubella (Anderson et al., 1985; Davidkin et al., 1998; De Los Ángeles Ribas et al., 2019; Rezaei et al., 2016), which produce a similar kind of rash and fever.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: It is possible that B19V might have been responsible for some of the numerous cases attributed to measles that were described in early 16th-century Mexico.
source: Therefore, it is possible that B19V might have been responsible for some of the numerous cases attributed to measles that were described in early 16th-century Mexico (Acuña-Soto et al., 2004; Mandujano-Sánchez et al., 1982; Wesp, 2017), in particular historical records that document the treatment of an outbreak of measles at the HSJN in 1531 CE (Meza, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to historical sources.

claim: Historical records document the treatment of an outbreak of measles at the HSJN in 1531 CE.
source: Therefore, it is possible that B19V might have been responsible for some of the numerous cases attributed to measles that were described in early 16th-century Mexico (Acuña-Soto et al., 2004; Mandujano-Sánchez et al., 1982; Wesp, 2017), in particular historical records that document the treatment of an outbreak of measles at the HSJN in 1531 CE (Meza, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Meza, 2013.

claim: Historical records of the autopsies of the victims of the 1576 CE Cocoliztli epidemic treated at the HSJN describe the presence of enlarged hard liver and jaundice.
source: Furthermore, historical records of the autopsies of the victims of the 1576 CE Cocoliztli epidemic treated at the HSJN describe the presence of enlarged hard liver and jaundice (Acuña-Soto et al., 2002; Acuña-Soto et al., 2004; Malvido and Viesca, 1982; Marr and Kiracofe, 2000; Somolinos d'Árdois, 1982) as well as a black spleen and lungs and heart with yellow liquid and black blood (Acuña-Soto et al., 2000; Malvido and Viesca, 1982; Somolinos d'Árdois, 1982).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to historical sources.

claim: Both HBV and B19V viruses proliferate in the liver and are associated with hepatitis and jaundice.
source: This is noteworthy given that both HBV and B19V viruses proliferate in the liver and are associated with hepatitis and jaundice (Broliden et al., 2006; Yuen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Broliden et al., 2006; Yuen et al., 2018.

claim: The radiocarbon dating of individuals HSJN194 and HSJN240 overlaps with the period of time when the hepatitis symptoms were reported in the autopsies after the 1576 Cocoliztli epidemic at the HSJN.
source: The radiocarbon dating of individuals HSJN194 (HBV) and HSJN240 (B19V) suggests that these individuals died between 1472–1625 CE and 1442–1608 CE (years calibrated for 1σ), respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), which overlaps with the period of time when the hepatitis symptoms were reported in the autopsies after the 1576 Cocoliztli epidemic at the HSJN (Acuña-Soto et al., 2004; Marr and Kiracofe, 2000; Somolinos d'Árdois, 1982).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and citations to historical sources.

claim: Both HBV and B19V have been previously identified in aDNA datasets not necessarily associated with disease or epidemic contexts.
source: Furthermore, it is important to acknowledge that both viruses have also been previously identified in aDNA datasets not necessarily associated with disease or epidemic contexts (Kahila Bar-Gal et al., 2012; Krause-Kyora et al., 2018; Mühlemann et al., 2018a; Patterson Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous ancient DNA studies.

claim: The transatlantic slave trade involved the forced displacement of millions of individuals to the Americas (ca. 250,000 to New Spain).
source: This cruel episode in history involved the forced displacement of millions of individuals to the Americas (ca. 250,000 to New Spain; Aguirre-Beltrán, 2005) under inhumane, unsanitary, and overcrowded conditions that, with no doubt, favored the spread of infectious diseases (Mandujano-Sánchez et al., 1982).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Aguirre-Beltrán, 2005; Mandujano-Sánchez et al., 1982.

claim: The inhumane, unsanitary, and overcrowded conditions of the transatlantic slave trade favored the spread of infectious diseases.
source: This cruel episode in history involved the forced displacement of millions of individuals to the Americas (ca. 250,000 to New Spain; Aguirre-Beltrán, 2005) under inhumane, unsanitary, and overcrowded conditions that, with no doubt, favored the spread of infectious diseases (Mandujano-Sánchez et al., 1982).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Mandujano-Sánchez et al., 1982.

claim: The introduction of HBV and B19V to the Americas should be attributed to the brutal and harsh conditions of the Middle passage that enslaved Africans were subjected to by traders and colonizers, and not to the African peoples themselves.
source: Therefore, the introduction of these and other pathogens from Africa to the Americas should be attributed to the brutal and harsh conditions of the Middle passage that enslaved Africans were subjected to by traders and colonizers, and not to the African peoples themselves.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an ethical clarification.

claim: The adverse life conditions for enslaved Africans and Native Americans, especially during the first decades after colonization, favored the spread of diseases and emergence of epidemics.
source: Moreover, the adverse life conditions for enslaved Africans and Native Americans, especially during the first decades after colonization, surely favored the spread of diseases and emergence of epidemics (Mandujano-Sánchez et al., 1982).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Mandujano-Sánchez et al., 1982.

claim: The isolation and characterization of ancient HBV and B19V genomes represent an important contribution to the ancient viral genomes reported in the Americas.
source: The isolation and characterization of these ancient HBV and B19V genomes represent an important contribution to the ancient viral genomes reported in the Americas (Barquera et al., 2020; Duggan et al., 2020; Schrick et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Barquera et al., 2020; Duggan et al., 2020; Schrick et al., 2017.

claim: The findings confirm that HBV and B19V were circulating in individuals found in archeological contexts associated with the Cocoliztli epidemic outbreak.
source: Although we cannot assign a direct causality link between HBV and B19V and Cocoliztli, our findings confirm that these potentially harmful viruses were indeed circulating in individuals found in archeological contexts associated with this epidemic outbreak.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Tooth roots can be a good source of pathogen DNA, especially in the case of viruses that are widespread in the bloodstream during systemic infection.
source: Tooth roots (which are vascularized) can be a good source of pathogen DNA (Key et al., 2017), especially in the case of viruses that are widespread in the bloodstream during systemic infection.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Key et al., 2017.

claim: A number of previous studies have successfully recovered ancient viral DNA from tooth roots.
source: Accordingly, a number of previous studies have successfully recovered ancient viral DNA from tooth roots (Barquera et al., 2020; Krause-Kyora et al., 2018; Mühlemann et al., 2020; Mühlemann et al., 2018a; Mühlemann et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to multiple studies.

claim: The study of ancient viral genomes has revealed important insights into the evolution of specific viral families.
source: The study of ancient viral genomes has revealed important insights into the evolution of specific viral families (Barquera et al., 2020; Duggan et al., 2016; Düx et al., 2020; Kahila Bar-Gal et al., 2012; Krause-Kyora et al., 2018; Mühlemann et al., 2018a; Mühlemann et al., 2018a; Mühlemann et al., 2018b; Neukamm et al., 2020; Pajer et al., 2017; Patterson Ross et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2013), as well as their interaction with human populations (Spyrou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with multiple citations.

claim: The study of ancient viral genomes has revealed important insights into their interaction with human populations.
source: The study of ancient viral genomes has revealed important insights into the evolution of specific viral families (Barquera et al., 2020; Duggan et al., 2016; Düx et al., 2020; Kahila Bar-Gal et al., 2012; Krause-Kyora et al., 2018; Mühlemann et al., 2018a; Mühlemann et al., 2018a; Mühlemann et al., 2018b; Neukamm et al., 2020; Pajer et al., 2017; Patterson Ross et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2013), as well as their interaction with human populations (Spyrou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation to Spyrou et al., 2019.

claim: The remains of a number of individuals in the HSJN collection displayed dental modifications and/or morphological indicators typical of African ancestry.
source: Prior bioarcheological research has shown that the remains of a number of individuals in the HSJN collection displayed dental modifications and/or morphological indicators typical of African ancestry (Meza, 2013), consistent with historical and archeological research that documents the presence of a large number of both free and enslaved Africans and their descendants in Colonial Mexico (Aguirre-Beltrán, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation to Meza, 2013.

claim: Historical and archeological research documents the presence of a large number of both free and enslaved Africans and their descendants in Colonial Mexico.
source: Prior bioarcheological research has shown that the remains of a number of individuals in the HSJN collection displayed dental modifications and/or morphological indicators typical of African ancestry (Meza, 2013), consistent with historical and archeological research that documents the presence of a large number of both free and enslaved Africans and their descendants in Colonial Mexico (Aguirre-Beltrán, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation to Aguirre-Beltrán, 2005.

claim: The African presence in the Indigenous Hospital might reflect an urgent response to an epidemic outbreak since hospitals treated patients regardless of the origin of the affected individuals during serious public health crises.
source: The African presence in the Indigenous Hospital might reflect an urgent response to an epidemic outbreak since hospitals treated patients regardless of the origin of the affected individuals during serious public health crises (Meza, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Meza, 2013.

claim: La Concepción chapel is located 10 km south of the HSJN in Coyoacán, a Pre-Hispanic Indigenous neighborhood that became the first Spanish settlement in Mexico City after the fall of Tenochtitlan.
source: Dental samples of five additional individuals were selected (based on their conservation state) from 'La Concepción' chapel (COY), which is located 10 km south of the HSJN in Coyoacán, a Pre-Hispanic Indigenous neighborhood that became the first Spanish settlement in Mexico City after the fall of Tenochtitlan (Moreno-Cabrera et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Moreno-Cabrera et al., 2015.

claim: The complex evolution of HBV may not be prone to appropriate genetic dating since multiple inter-genotype recombination and cross-species transmission (Human-Ape) events occurred throughout its evolution.
source: The complex evolution of HBV may not be prone to an appropriate genetic dating since multiple inter-genotype recombination and cross-species transmission (Human-Ape) events (Krause-Kyora et al., 2018) occurred throughout its evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Krause-Kyora et al., 2018.

claim: The entire HBV genotype A has been identified as a recombinant genotype.
source: Since the entire genotype A has been identified as a recombinant genotype before (Mühlemann et al., 2018a), we analyzed it independently and identified a stronger temporal signal within this genotype (R2 = 0.722; correlation coefficient = 0.8498) (Figure 3—figure supplement 5d-f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Mühlemann et al., 2018a.

claim: A stronger temporal signal was identified within HBV genotype A (R2 = 0.722; correlation coefficient = 0.8498).
source: Since the entire genotype A has been identified as a recombinant genotype before (Mühlemann et al., 2018a), we analyzed it independently and identified a stronger temporal signal within this genotype (R2 = 0.722; correlation coefficient = 0.8498) (Figure 3—figure supplement 5d-f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 5d-f.

claim: Little or no temporal structure was found for the HBV phylogeny containing all genotypes (R2 = 0.1351; correlation coefficient = 0.3676).
source: Similarly to previous studies (Krause-Kyora et al., 2018; Patterson Ross et al., 2018), we found little or no temporal structure for this HBV phylogeny containing all genotypes (R2 = 0.1351; correlation coefficient = 0.3676) (Figure 3—figure supplement 5a-c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 5a-c and citations to previous studies.
